newsitem.title: USA: At Home shares soars in stock market debut.
newsitem.headline: At Home shares soars in stock market debut.

text.p: The stock of high-speed Internet access provider At Home Corp. soared on its first day of trading Friday, briefly valuing the money-losing start-up company at nearly $3 billion.

After the initial jump, some analysts compared it to the initial public offering (IPO) of Netscape Communications Corp., whose stock soared as high as $75 from $28 on its first day of trading and sparked investor euphoria over Internet stocks.

"I think the company's probably more valuable than Netscape in many ways," said Steve Harmon, an analyst at Mecklermedia's iWorld investment service. "People are betting on cable as the killer application of the Internet."

At Home pushed as high as $25.50 in early trading, but retreated to close at $17, up $6.50, on volume of more than 12.6 million shares on Nasdaq. The company's stock was sold to underwriters at $10.50 a share in its initial public offering late on Thursday, raising $94.5 million in total proceeds.

By any measure, analysts said the stock price was heady for a start-up that lost $24.5 million last year on sales of just $676,000 as it began rolling out its services to a few thousand subscribers in a handful of communities.

But this is no garage operation, with backing from cable television giants such as Tele-Communications Inc., Comcast Corp., and Cox Communications Inc., in addition to high profile venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers.

By using its own high-speed network, the Redwood City, Calif.-based company said it can provide continuous Internet access via cable modem connections at speeds more than 300 times faster than typical telephone dial-up connections.

With about 117.5 million shares outstanding, the IPO valued At Home at more than $1.2 billion. Friday's peak market price valued the company at $2.99 billion while its closing price made its worth about $1.99 billion.
The first day performance set no records, but provided a rich valuation for a company that has said it expects to produce "substantial" losses for the foreseeable future.

It also attracted Intel Corp., which bought about $5 million worth of stock at $10.50 a share, sources familiar with the transaction said. An Intel spokesman declined to say if the company but stock but noted Intel has been talking with At Home since it began in 1995.

Analysts said At Home was set to take advantage of consumer frustration over slow Internet dial-up speeds and deliver more compelling services that will be easier to use -- which would in turn increase the speed of consumer acceptance.

At Home's cable partners can reach as many as 44 million homes, but some analysts said it was not known if enough consumers would be willing to pay an anticipated $35 to $55 a month for online services.
"The potential is all there, (but) most people should look at it as a development-stage company," said IPO Maven editor and publisher Manish Shah. "It's speculative in many ways."
Scott Ryles, managing director of the technology group at Merrill Lynch, which co-led the offering with Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, said the deal was oversubscribed, but did not say by how much.
"The service won't be mature for another three to five years, but their business model is very well defined and the technology has been well deployed. We know it works," he said.

Henry Nicholas, chief executive officer of Broadcom Corp., which develops chips for communications gear, said At Home's service was a great improvement. "Boom. You're right on," he said, comparing it to slow dialup access. "It's the first service where they have customers calling them up, beating on the door."
